title: URL shortener
summary: Key generation, read-heavy caching and redirects.
prompt: Design a URL shortener. Users paste a long URL and get a short link; anyone opening the short link is redirected. Support optional custom aliases, link expiry and basic click counts for the owner.

requirements: Functional: create a short link (optional custom alias and expiry), redirect, and show click counts to the owner.
Non-functional: redirects are read-heavy and latency-sensitive (tens of ms server-side), highly available, and a code never silently changes target.
Out of scope unless asked: rich analytics dashboards, link editing, full account management.
estimation: 100M new links a month ≈ 40 writes/s on average (100M ÷ 2.6M seconds); plan for 5× peaks.
At 100 reads per write, redirects average ~4,000/s and peak near 20,000/s.
5 years × 1.2B links/year = 6B links; at ~500 bytes each that is about 3 TB.
Seven base62 characters give 62⁷ ≈ 3.5 trillion codes, far more than 6B.
api: POST /links {url, alias?, expiresAt?} with an Idempotency-Key → 201 {code, shortUrl}; 409 if the alias is taken.
GET /{code} → 302 with Location header; 404 for unknown and 410 for expired codes.
data: links(code PK, long_url, owner_id, created_at, expires_at): a pure key-value access pattern.
A secondary index on owner_id serves “my links”; nothing on the redirect path needs a join.
Click counts live in a separate counter table fed by events, so redirects never write to the links row.
design: Clients → CDN/edge → load balancer → stateless link service → cache → links store.
Create: the service takes the next ID from a block it leased from an ID allocator, base62-encodes it and inserts the row.
Redirect: cache lookup, then store on a miss; each redirect emits a click event to a queue that a counter worker aggregates in batches.
deepDives: Key generation: each server leases blocks of, say, 10,000 IDs, so creating a link needs no coordination. Random codes with insert-if-absent also work but need collision retries.
Sequential IDs make codes guessable; apply a reversible permutation to the ID before encoding if enumeration matters.
301 vs 302: a 301 is cached by browsers, which cuts load but hides clicks and makes expiry unreliable; a 302 keeps every click visible.
Popularity is heavily skewed, so caching the hottest few percent of codes serves most redirects. Briefly cache “not found” too, to absorb scans of invalid codes.
bottlenecks: Viral links: edge caching with a short max-age plus an in-process cache on each server.
Abuse: rate-limit creation per user and IP, check targets against malware and phishing lists, and disable (not delete) flagged codes.
Allocator outage only blocks new links once leased blocks run out; run it replicated.
tradeoffs: Leased ID blocks waste IDs when a server crashes. That is harmless with trillions of codes and buys coordination-free writes.
Click counts lag by seconds, which keeps the redirect path read-only.
Custom aliases share the keyspace with generated codes; a conditional insert settles races either way.

rubric.text: Quantified read and write rates and storage, and sized the code space.
Chose a key-generation scheme and explained how it avoids collisions.
Explained 301 vs 302 and the effect on click counts.
Kept click counting off the redirect write path.
Addressed abuse: malicious targets and enumeration of sequential codes.
Named failure modes (allocator outage, cache loss) and their blast radius.
